newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Stability a worry in Asia drive to economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Stability a worry in Asia drive to economic reform.

text.p: Economic policymakers urged Asia on Friday to continue its drive towards economic liberalisation but said social stability remains a worry in the region amid extremes of grinding poverty and opulent wealth.

"Economic growth has to be integrated into the overall philosophy of human development," Malaysian Minister of Finance Anwar Ibrahim told a Hong Kong Monetary Authority International Monetary Fund (IMF) conference.

"A global and supposedly free market which marginalises the many while it benefits the few, which serves in the interests of the rich and powerful while ignoring the legitimate needs of the poor and weak, which creates islands of wealth amidst a sea of poverty will certainly jeopardise the future of our children and grandchildren," he said.

The theme of Friday's one-day conference -- financial integration in Asia and the role of Hong Kong -- had central bankers from Hong Kong, China, the Philippines, Malaysia and Korea praising the merits of liberalisation.

"Much of Asia's dynamism can be traced to the openness of its economies and to the competitiveness and transfer of technology that this openness has encouraged," said IMF managing director Michel Camdessus.
He urged countries which had not yet opened their economies significantly to do so.
"Labour market flexibility will be critical to how successful these economies deal with the challenges of globalisation," added David Goldsbrough, senior advisor, Asia and Pacific Department, IMF.

"Rather than attempting to limit the pace of globalisation... the appropriate policy response is instead to address the underlying structural rigidities that prevent labor markets from adjusting to external shocks or technological change," he said.
Camdessus said countries would "need to develop effective exit policies for noncompetitive industries".
Structural changes would also have to come about without unduly restraining public finances or external positions.

"What is required for the success to continue is more of the same: macroeconomic stability and policies to enhance growth," said David Borthwick, deputy secretary at Australia's Department of the Treasury.
"But to say that is easy. The task, as policy makers know all too well, is formidable...Success in one area can bring problems in another," he said.

Goldsbrough said nations should look to Hong Kong as an example. Hong Kong follows a determinedly laissez-faire policy. Last year, it was voted the world's freest economy by right-wing American thinktank the Heritage Foundation.

"Those are difficult issues," he said. "I think they can look to Hong Kong and the way things have been dealt with in Hong Kong - massive structural changes being handled in a manner that has not created great economic disruptions."
Hong Kong has evolved from a mainly manufacturing centre to a service economy in less than a generation.
